claim: DeepFly3D infers the 3D pose of tethered, adult Drosophila using multiple camera images.
source: Here, we present DeepFly3D, a software that infers the 3D pose of tethered, adult Drosophila using multiple camera images.

claim: DeepFly3D does not require manual calibration.
source: DeepFly3D does not require manual calibration, uses pictorial structures to automatically detect and correct pose estimation errors, and uses active learning to iteratively improve performance.

source: The precise quantification of movements is critical for understanding how neurons, biomechanics, and the environment influence and give rise to animal behaviors.

claim: Modern approaches can simultaneously record the activity of neural populations in tethered, behaving animals.
source: Paired with modern approaches to simultaneously record the activity of neural populations in tethered, behaving animals (Dombeck et al., 2007; Seelig et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2018), 3D joint and appendage tracking promises to accelerate the discovery of neural control principles, particularly in the genetically tractable and numerically simple nervous system of the fly, Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: 3D joint and appendage tracking promises to accelerate the discovery of neural control principles in Drosophila melanogaster.

evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the potential impact of the technology.

claim: Small markers (reflective, colored, or fluorescent particles) can be used to identify and reconstruct keypoints from video data.

claim: The marker-based approach works well on humans.
source: Although this approach works well on humans (Moeslund and Granum, 2000), in smaller, Drosophila-sized animals markers likely hamper movements and are difficult to mount on sub-millimeter scale limbs.

claim: In Drosophila-sized animals, markers likely hamper movements and are difficult to mount on sub-millimeter scale limbs.

source: Before the advent of deep learning, this was accomplished by matching the contours of animals seen against uniform backgrounds (Isakov et al., 2016), measuring limb tip positions using complex TIRF-based imaging approaches (Mendes et al., 2013), or measuring limb segments using active contours (Uhlmann et al., 2017).

evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work using this method.

source: Individual flies were recorded for five trials each, with one-minute intervals.

claim: The unsupervised behavioral classification approach mostly followed the approach taken by Todd et al. (2017) and Berman et al. (2014).

source: We smoothed 3D pose traces using a 1€ filter.

source: Then we converted them into angles to achieve scale and translational invariance (Casiez et al., 2012).

claim: Angles were calculated by taking the dot product from sets of three connected 3D positions.
source: Angles were calculated by taking the dot product from sets of three connected 3D positions.

claim: For the antennae, the angle of the line defined by two antennal points with respect to the ground-plane was calculated.

source: This way, we generated four angles per leg (two body-coxa, one coxa-femur, and one femur-tibia), two angles for the abdomen (top and bottom abdominal stripes), and a single angle for the antennae (head tilt with respect to the axis of gravity). In total, we obtained a set of 20 angles, extracted from 38 3D points.

source: We transformed angular time series using a Continous Wavelet Transform (CWT) to create a posture-dynamics space.

claim: The Morlet Wavelet was used as the mother wavelet.
source: We used the Morlet Wavelet as the mother wavelet, given its suitability to isolate periodic chirps of motion.

claim: 25 wavelet scales were chosen to match dyadically spaced center frequencies between 5 Hz and 50 Hz.
source: We chose 25 wavelet scales to match dyadically spaced center frequencies between 5 Hz and 50 Hz.
evidence: This describes the wavelet scale selection.

claim: Spectrograms were calculated for each postural time-series by taking the magnitudes of the wavelet coefficients.
source: Then, we calculatd spectrograms for each postural time-series by taking the magnitudes of the wavelet coefficients.
evidence: This describes the spectrogram calculation method.

claim: This yields a 20 × 25 = 500-dimensional time-series.
source: This yields a 20 × 25 = 500-dimensional time-series, which was then normalized over all frequency channels to unit length, at each time instance.

source: This yields a 20 × 25 = 500-dimensional time-series, which was then normalized over all frequency channels to unit length, at each time instance.

claim: A two-dimensional representation of behavior was computed using the non-linear embedding algorithm, t-SNE.
source: Later, from the posture-dynamics space, we computed a two-dimensional representation of behavior by using the non-linear embedding algorithm, t-SNE (Maaten, 2008).
evidence: This describes the dimensionality reduction method, supported by citation.

source: t-SNE embedded our high-dimensional posture-dynamics space onto a 2D plane, while preserving the high-dimensional local structure, while sacrificing larger scale accuracy.

source: We used the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence as the distance function in our t-SNE algorithm.

claim: A perplexity value of 35 was empirically found to best suit the features of the posture-dynamics space.
source: By analyzing a multitude of plots generated with different perplexity values, we empirically found a perplexity value of 35 to best suit the features of our posture-dynamics space.

source: From this generated discrete space, we created a continuous 2D distribution, that we could then segment into behavioral clusters. We started by normalizing the 2D t-SNE projected space into a 1000 × 1000 matrix.

claim: The space was segmented by inverting it and applying a Watershed algorithm that separated adjacent basins, yielding a behavioral map.
